newsitem.title: CANADA: Mounties smash human smuggling ring in Canada, U.S..
newsitem.headline: Mounties smash human smuggling ring in Canada, U.S..

text.p: Police said on Wednesday they had broken up a sophisticated ring that smuggled Asians into North America where they were ultimately enslaved in prostitution, gambling and sweatshops.

After a year-long investigation, Canadian Mounties and other U.S. and international authorities struck in the early hours of Tuesday, rounding up 13 people alleged to be involved in the ring in Toronto, Vancouver and Hong Kong.
The Asian syndicate was believed to be smuggling some 30 to 40 people from various Southeast Asian countries into Canada, where they would be slipped across the border to the United States.
"The investigation has had a major impact on this syndicate," Royal Canadian Mounted Police Sergeant Vern Secord told a news conference on Wednesday.
Secord said the ring was a sophisticated operation bringing Asians into the Canadian ports of Montreal and Vancouver via South America.

They were usually brought to Toronto, Canada's largest city, and kept in safe houses, sometimes against their will, until they could be smuggled across the border of Ontario and New York state in the trunks of cars. Most of the aliens ended up in New York City, the authorities said.
Michael McLaughlin, assistant director with U.S. Immigration, said the aliens paid $30,000 to $35,000 each for the illegal passage to North America.

He said a portion of the money was paid up front by the individuals or members of their family, and anything left unpaid was recovered through "slave labor" in fields such as prostitution, gambling and sweatshops.
"If they made it to the United States, I'm sure the smugglers are still keeping them under control," McLaughlin told a news conference.

Canadian Immigration spokeswoman Lucille Leblanc said they believed many of the illegal aliens initially entered Canada by claiming status as a refugee. Canada allows easier access to those that can prove they are being persecuted for political or other reasons in their home country.
"It's a worldwide problem, one that all countries have to deal with," she said.
